clinicalPearls: Chronic kidney disease caused by prolonged lead exposure, producing a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy
It is classically associated with hyperuricaemia and gout (saturnine gout) and with hypertension
Acute high-dose exposure in children can cause a reversible proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi-type) with lead inclusion bodies
Sources include occupational exposure, old lead paint and pipes, contaminated traditional remedies and illicit alcohol
Blood lead reflects recent exposure; body burden may be assessed with a chelation-mobilisation test where available
Management is removal from exposure and treatment of hypertension, with chelation for significant lead burden
reference.pathophysiology: Lead nephropathy results from accumulation of lead in renal tubular cells, where it impairs mitochondrial and enzymatic function and, with chronic exposure, causes tubulointerstitial fibrosis and progressive chronic kidney disease. Lead also reduces renal urate excretion, producing hyperuricaemia and gout, and contributes to hypertension, which further damages the kidney. In acute childhood poisoning, lead causes a proximal tubular dysfunction with characteristic intranuclear inclusion bodies that is often reversible.
additionalDifferentials: Other chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathies (analgesic, aristolochic acid)
Chronic kidney disease of other aetiology
additionalInvestigations: Blood lead level and exposure history
Assessment of renal function, urate and blood pressure
Lead-mobilisation (chelation) test for body burden where indicated
Urinalysis and markers of tubular dysfunction
redFlags: Progressive chronic kidney disease with ongoing exposure
Features of systemic lead toxicity (neurological, anaemia)
reference.prognosis: Removing exposure and controlling hypertension can stabilise renal function, and acute childhood tubulopathy may reverse, but established chronic interstitial fibrosis is irreversible.
pitfalls: Overlooking lead as a cause of chronic kidney disease with gout and hypertension
Failing to take an occupational and environmental exposure history
Relying only on blood lead, which reflects recent rather than cumulative exposure
